title: What the Soviet Union Did to Planet Earth
description:

For seventy years, the Soviet Union tried to rebuild the planet itself: it drained a sea to grow cotton, set off more than 120 "peaceful" nuclear explosions, some to dig lakes and canals, planned to turn Siberia's rivers around, and heard proposals to melt the Arctic. title: Two Empty Bowls Beat Sixteen Horses
description:
Sixteen horses could not pull two copper bowls apart.

Otto von Guericke, the mayor of Magdeburg, built an air pump in the 1650s and used it to pump the air out of two copper hemispheres about half a metre across. The air outside then pressed the halves together with about 20,000 newtons, roughly two tonnes of weight, and teams of horses could not separate them. When the valve opened and air flowed back in, they fell apart.

The maths: air pressure about 100,000 N per square metre x the bowl's open face about 0.2 square metres = about 20,000 N. A second team of horses adds nothing: a tree on one side would have held the same pull.

Anselm the coppersmith, Jost the horse master and the crowd are invented for the story (illustrative). The experiment and the physics are real.

title: What if you were a snowflake that couldn't stop being buried?
description:
You are one snowflake. You form in a cloud, fall on the East Antarctic plateau and the snow keeps coming. This is the whole journey: the first night under the surface, the layers that count the years, the moment air gets sealed into a bubble, the pressure of three kilometres of ice, the slow creep toward the sea, the crack that stops 30 metres short, the break, the iceberg and the way back into a cloud.

What is real and what is not:
- The place is Dome C, where the EPICA ice core was drilled. The ages and depths in the corner follow that core's published chronology (EDC3): the ice at 100 m is about 2,500 years old and the bubbles seal there; 363 m is 11,700 years; 503 m is 20,000; 3,188 m is 800,000 years.
- You fall today, so older layers lie below you and sink as fast as you do. You never reach them. The volcano layer in the video is the eruption of Tambora in 1815, which left acid in Antarctic ice. The depth shown (about 11 m) is an estimate.
- Carbon dioxide in the bubbles: ice-age air held about 190 parts per million, the air before factories about 280, and over 800,000 years of ice cores never went above 300. The air in your own bubble would be today's: 424.6 ppm in 2024 (NOAA, Mauna Loa).

title: How a Thin Tube Burst a Barrel
description:
Bram says he can burst a strong barrel with one jug of water. Harl the barrel-maker laughs and bets his lid. Then Bram climbs a very tall ladder with a very thin pipe.

The trick is real physics: the pressure in still water depends on how tall the water stands, not on how much of it there is. About ten metres of water pushes with roughly the pressure of the whole atmosphere, so a thin pipe standing ten metres tall can split a barrel. The story and the people are made up. A famous version of this experiment is credited to Blaise Pascal in 1646, but historians doubt it happened as told. The pipe is drawn much wider than a real one so it shows on a phone.

The sound is generated and the narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro text to speech).

Sources: HyperPhysics (Georgia State), "Fluid Pressure"; Wikipedia "Hydrostatic pressure", "Atmospheric pressure", "Pascal's barrel".

title: What if you were trapped inside the Sun for 100,000 years?
description:
You are a particle of light, born in the middle of the Sun. The light that reaches your eyes took about 8 minutes to cross space, but it spent far longer getting out of the Sun itself. This is that trip, step by step: the core, the random walk through the radiative zone, the boiling layer, the surface, then Parker Solar Probe, Mercury, Venus, Earth, the space station, the air and finally a human eye.

What is real and what is not:
- The 100,000 years is an estimate for how long energy takes to work its way out. Published values run from about 10,000 to 170,000 years or more, depending on the model (Mitalas and Sills, 1992, gave about 170,000). The video uses 100,000 and says the age readout is an estimate.
- It is not really one photon. Light is absorbed and re-emitted trillions upon trillions of times, and each hit can split the energy into weaker light. The video says so: you are energy, passed along.
- The path is a random walk, so the number of steps is huge: roughly a trillion trillion. A neutrino, which hardly ever hits anything, crosses the Sun in about 2 seconds.
- Temperatures, densities, layer depths, the 5-minute pulses and the sizes of granules are from NASA and solar physics references (see the fact table in the folder). The time in the boiling layer is only a rough guess and is marked as one.
- Parker Solar Probe really passed 6.1 million km above the Sun's surface on 24 December 2024 at 692,000 km/h.
- Travel times from the Sun are real: Mercury about 3 minutes

title: Why Roman Bridges Still Stand After 1,900 Years
description:
A made-up legend about a mason, a proud engineer and a flat stone slab, and the real reason a stone arch holds. Stone is strong when squeezed and weak when stretched. A flat slab is stretched on its underside and cracks. An arch turns the weight into a squeeze that runs from stone to stone. The Alcantara Bridge in Spain is about 1,900 years old and still standing.

What is real and what is not:
- Real: stone is strong when squeezed and weak when stretched, a loaded flat slab cracks on its stretched underside, an arch carries load as a squeeze with the banks pushing back, the Romans built arch bridges that still stand, and the Alcantara Bridge was built about 104 to 106 AD.
- Made up: the town, the mason Gaius, the engineer Lucius, the test day and the sparrow. The models on the table bend far more than real stone would, to make the stretch easy to see.

The narrator is a text-to-speech voice (Kokoro). The sound effects are generated from scratch. No music.

description:

title: What if your money doubled every 2 seconds?
description:

A $100 bill weighs 1 gram, so $1 million is 10 kg. Double it 29 times and you have $537 trillion: about 5.4 million tonnes of $100 bills. Packed solid, that is a block 182 m wide, taller than the Great Pyramid. The world's total wealth was about $471 trillion at the end of 2024.

The start amount and the timing are illustrative. The size of the pile assumes $100 bills with no air gaps.

title: What if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted near you?
description:
What if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted and you lived near it?

Yellowstone's last caldera-forming eruption was about 640,000 years ago. The USGS says the volcano is not overdue for another and puts the chance of one in any given year at roughly 1 in 730,000. Nothing at Yellowstone points to an eruption soon, and the USGS monitors it every day.

If one did happen, USGS ash-fall modelling of a 330 cubic kilometre supereruption (lasting from 3 days to a month, depending on the run) shows ash decimetres to metres deep across the northern Rockies, centimetres to decimetres in the northern Midwest, and millimetres to centimetres on the East, West and Gulf coasts. The USGS adds that the accumulation, though widespread and substantial, is far less than in most doomsday scenarios. For comparison, Mount St. Helens in 1980 put out about 0.3 cubic miles (1.3 cubic km) of ash before it compacted.

The countdown, the distance and the arrival time here are made up. Real timing depends on how far you are and which way the wind blows, so the readout is labelled illustrative. The plume, the lightning inside it and the ash ceiling are simplified. Pyroclastic flows are left out on purpose: the USGS says the parts of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming closest to Yellowstone would get them, and places farther away would get falling ash.

title: What If You Sped Up and Couldn’t Stop?
description:
Something goes wrong and you start speeding up, and it doesn't stop. You outrun traffic on your own street, then a bullet train, an airliner and your own sound. The ground drops away under you. You pass the Moon in fifteen seconds, the Sun in half a minute, and then your speed sticks just under the speed of light and something else gives way instead: time.

The readout in the corner is your speed the whole way. The numbers are real: sound travels at 1,235 km/h, staying in orbit takes about 28,000 km/h, and leaving Earth takes about 40,000. The Moon is 384,400 kilometres away and the Sun is 150 million, eight minutes away for light. The nearest star is 4.25 light-years out, the Orion nebula about 1,300, Andromeda 2.5 million and the Virgo cluster 54 million. Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light, but the closer you get, the slower your own clock runs, so the second readout is real too: it shows how far the clocks at home have run ahead of yours.

Some of it is not real. The dust and the stars streaking past between galaxies are there so you can see yourself move, everything is lined up along one straight path, and at these speeds the whole sky would really be squeezed into one blinding point ahead of you. Galaxies more than about 16 billion light-years away can never be reached, even at the speed of light, because the space in between is stretching too fast. The very last thing that happens is made up.

title: What If You Grew and Couldn't Stop?
description:
Something goes wrong and you start growing, and it doesn't stop. You go through your own roof, rise past a news helicopter and up through the clouds, then stand with your head in space, the Earth between your shoes, the Sun a spark, the Milky Way turning around your ankles, and finally the edge of everything anyone has ever seen at your waist.

The readout in the corner is your size the whole way up. The sizes are real: space begins about 100 kilometres up, the space station flies at about 400, the Earth is 12,742 kilometres wide, the Moon is 384,400 kilometres away, and the Sun is 150 million, so far that its light takes eight minutes to arrive. The nearest star is about 4 light-years away, the Milky Way is roughly 100,000 light-years across, and Andromeda is 2.5 million light-years away. Where the stars and galaxies sit around you is arranged for the camera, and nothing real could grow this fast or survive it. The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. Nobody knows what is outside it, so the video stops there.

You started about 10²⁷ times smaller than the observable universe, and about 10³⁵ times bigger than the smallest length physics can describe. You were always closer to the top.

Victor wakes up reborn as Izuku Midoriya’s twin brother, with a quirk that turns everything he takes into an S-rank power. But this isn’t a “the main character just wins” story. Bakugo lost his quirk for one minute and never forgot it. The Hero Public Safety Commission wants to lock Victor away. Izuku Midoriya lived through everything: One For All, the final war, losing his quirk, coming back as a hero in a support suit. Then he dies on a rescue at twenty eight and wakes up as a baby. Same mother, same apartment, same world. Only this time Inko has a daughter, Izumi, and she remembers all of it.

No quirk again. A grown hero stuck in a little girl’s body. And a head full of the future. Toya on Sekoto Peak, All Might’s fight with All For One, Stain, Garaki, Eri. She knows when and where all of it happens. The question is what a four year old can actually do about it, and how much the world changes once she starts.

This is my own original story. I wrote the whole thing from scratch: the plot, the timeline, how every character reacts to the changes, the ending. It’s not a retelling of the anime with a few things swapped. Once one thing changes, everything after it changes too. Kacchan, All Might, Tenko, the League, UA, it all goes differently. I spent a lot of time on the writing, working out the characters and their designs, the visuals and the editing, so I hope you enjoy it.

title: He Ground Every Train Wheel Crooked on Purpose. Everyone Laughed. #shorts #animation
description:
A foreman shaves perfectly good train wheels into cones. His rival grinds his wheels flat as drums and laughs at him. Then comes the first sharp bend. A coned wheel has a wide edge and a narrow edge: when a wheelset slides sideways on a curve, the outside wheel rides its wide edge and covers more ground than the inside wheel, so the axle turns itself into the bend. No steering, no driver input. The lip (flange) is only a backup and usually does not touch the rail in normal running.

Real mechanism, told with invented characters and staging. The foreman, the rival, the yard and the quotes are ours, and the derailment is a comic illustration, not a claim that flat wheels derail instantly (they would mostly scrub and wear). The paper cup trick works the same way.

Would you have bet on flat or cone?

title: The Skyscraper They Fixed in Secret #shorts #animation
description:
Every night in 1978, welders slipped into a brand-new New York skyscraper after the office went home.

The 59-story tower stood on giant stilts, and a student's question about wind from its corners sent its designer back to his sums. His welded joints had been swapped for bolts, and by his numbers, one big storm could knock it down.

So the crews welded steel plates over about 200 joints, night after night. Then, halfway through, a hurricane headed for the city.

The storm turned out to sea, the newspapers were on strike, and the full story stayed out of the public eye for 17 years.

Would you have told everyone, or kept quiet and fixed it?

True story, told with invented cartoon characters. The office laughing, the jokes and all spoken lines are dramatized. The danger is what the engineer calculated at the time; a 2020 reassessment found the corner-wind loads less of a threat than he feared.

title: The Bounty That Bred Rats #shorts #animation
description:

This is the story of the Great Hanoi Rat Massacre, and the oldest lesson in incentive design: pay for the proof and people will manufacture the proof.

The scene, characters and dialogue are dramatised. The core history is real: the sewers of colonial Hanoi, the one-cent tail bounty, hunters turning in tails instead of whole rats, tailless rats seen running around the city, and reports of rat breeding outside the city to keep the payments coming.

title: What If You Could Leave Your Body and Drive Anyone?
description:
You're inside Mr. Pruitt's golden retriever, dunking his slipper in a birdbath while your own body slides toward a pool. If you could leave your body and drive anyone, who would keep you safe?

You're Stelvo, and three heartbeats let you take control of someone you can see, even on a live camera. Their hands keep their skills, but their knowledge stays locked away. In this fictional story, body swapping makes almost anything feel possible. The problem is that every ride leaves something behind—and takes a little of you with it.

From a darts champion and a disastrous chess match, to a billionaire's boardroom, a forgotten handshake and your mom's terrifying flight—each new ride brings you closer to losing the person you came home to.

title: What If Your Parent's IQ Got Much Worse Every Second?
description:
What if your parent's IQ got much worse every second? Your dad's IQ starts at 100, exactly average, and drops one point a minute, down past 40 to zero at 6:00, when Mom gets home.

It's Saturday, 4:20 PM. Dad has just lit the grill and he's labelling things with sticky notes. He can't read the clock. He points the TV remote at himself, then holds it to his ear like a phone. Mom calls: don't let him near the stove. He finds the stove. You call Grandpa, who isn't getting involved. You order a pizza; Dad pays the driver with a sticky note that says MONEY. You call 911: is anyone hurt? No. Then the line is for emergencies. The neighbor looks over the wall: not my yard, kid. The police come to the door: it's his house, no crime, no danger. Dad salutes the officer with a spatula. He labels the whole house, then he labels you. The fat catches. Mom texts: turning onto our street.

The numbers are real. IQ tests are scored so the average adult is 100, with a standard deviation of 15: about 2 in 3 adults score between 85 and 115. The "how rare" card is that bell curve: one adult in so many scores this low, set against the 8.2 billion people alive (UN, 2024). Real tests stop measuring at about 40 (the WAIS-IV reports 40 to 160); below that the number is only the curve's. 911 is for anyone who needs police, fire or an ambulance right now; the US gets about 240 million 911 calls a year (NENA estimate). title: What If Your Sink Couldn't Stop Running?
description:
What if your sink couldn't stop running? Your kitchen faucet's flow, in gallons a minute, climbs from 2.2 gal/min, the most a faucet is allowed, past a fire hose and a fire hydrant to over 5,000 gal/min: five fire hydrants.

It's a Saturday afternoon and the sink is full. You push the lever down. It doesn't turn off. It gets stronger. So you try everything. Your palm over the spout. The two shut-off valves under the sink. The main shut-off in the garage, which turns off every pipe in the house: the pipes knock, and it keeps coming. You open the front door to let it out. You open the spigot outside: not a drop, your pipes are empty. You cap the faucet with your coffee mug and it's torn out of your hand. You push the lever the other way. You twist the spout off, and the water goes straight up into the ceiling. You open the big garage door to let the water out of the garage. Your water app says you've used 0 gallons today. So you go out to the meter by the sidewalk and lift its lid. It isn't moving.

The numbers are real. A new kitchen faucet may pass at most 2.2 gal/min (8.3 L/min) at 60 psi under US federal rules (10 CFR 430.32), a shower head 2.5. A household 5/8 x 3/4 in water meter measures up to about 20 gal/min, and a house's own service rarely carries more than 25-30. title: What If You Got Older and Couldn't Stop?
description:
It's your 25th birthday. Mom texts: breakfast at the diner at 9:00, three blocks away. You step off your porch at 8:51, and you start getting older. Slowly at first, then a year every two seconds, then faster. For everyone else on the street it's an ordinary nine-minute walk to breakfast. For you it's a whole life, then the longest life anyone has ever lived, then longer than anything alive.

All of it is one shot, through your own eyes. Watch your hands.

What's real: every age on the ladder (the average American life, 79 years; Jeanne Calment, the oldest person ever, 122 years and 164 days; Jonathan the tortoise, 193 and still alive; a bowhead whale, 211; the United States, 250; a Greenland shark, 392; Ming the clam, 507; Methuselah, the oldest tree alive, about 4,858), how close your eyes can focus at each age, how many times a heart beats in a year (about 38 million), how slowly people walk past eighty, how crosswalks are timed (3.5 feet a second), how the eye's lens yellows, and how hearing goes from the top down.

description:
An October evening on a farm in Kansas. Your footprints in the dust are getting fainter, because you're getting lighter, and you can't stop. A gust knocks you over. title: What If It Got Colder and Couldn't Stop?
description:
You're standing on your dock on a mild autumn afternoon when the temperature starts to fall, and it never stops. Your lake freezes from the posts outward. Your breath freezes with a tinkle. A tree splits like a gunshot. You pass the coldest temperature ever measured on Earth, watch carbon dioxide fall as snow, and then the air itself turns to liquid and rains down, filling the valley until your dock, the cabins and most of the forest are gone. Then it freezes too. And it keeps going, all the way down towards absolute zero.

What's real: every rung on the ladder is a real temperature. Water freezes at 0 °C; °C and °F agree at −40; the coldest air ever measured was −89.2 °C at Vostok station in 1983, and satellites have seen −98 °C on the Antarctic snow. Today's air would snow out its carbon dioxide at about −141 °C (about 4 mm of dry ice if you froze all of it). Air starts to turn liquid at −191.4 °C, oxygen first, which is pale blue; nitrogen boils at −195.8 °C, freezes at −210 °C, and oxygen freezes at −218.8 °C. All the air on Earth, as a liquid, would be 11.9 m deep. Empty space is 2.7 K (−270.4 °C), the Boomerang Nebula about 1 K, and absolute zero, −273.15 °C, can be approached but never reached. Sources for every number are in the project's notes.

title: What If You Got Heavier and Couldn't Stop?
description:

The scale gives up, the floor bends and drops you into the kitchen, and out in your street the pavement sinks under your feet. You go down past the gas pipe, the water main and a shark's tooth in the clay, fall into a tube tunnel just before a train, and keep going: through chalk, granite and the hot rock where diamonds are made, into an ocean of liquid iron, all the way to the very centre of the Earth. And you are still getting heavier.

The crust is about 35 km thick, the mantle goes down to 2,890 km, then comes the liquid iron of the outer core (its currents make the Earth a magnet), and from 5,150 km the solid inner core, as hot as the surface of the Sun. The centre is 6,371 km down. At 147 million tonnes your own pull, a metre from you, is as strong as the Earth's. title: What If You Shrank and Couldn't Stop?
description:
A sunny afternoon in your back garden, and you start to shrink. You can't stop. The grass closes over your head, a robin hunts right past you, and an ant comes up and feels you with its antennae. A drop of water slides down a blade of grass and swallows you. Inside it: a water bear, a paramecium, glass diatoms. Then bacteria, viruses, the inside of a cell, the DNA, one carbon atom, its nucleus, one proton, its quarks, and further down than anyone has ever measured.

What is real: every size on screen and the things that live at each size. A robin is about 14 cm long, a garden ant about 4.5 mm, a water bear about half a millimetre, a paramecium a quarter of a millimetre, E. coli about 2 thousandths of a millimetre, the virus (a T4 phage) about 200 nanometres, a ribosome 21 nm, the DNA 2 nm wide, a carbon atom about 0.34 nm, its nucleus about 5 femtometres and a proton 1.7 femtometres across. No experiment has ever found a size for a quark: it is smaller than 0.0000000000000000004 m, if it has a size at all. The walk back to your door is real arithmetic: 8 metres, with your steps shrinking as you do. By the end it would take longer than the universe has existed.

What is not real, or not known: nobody can shrink. Below the size of a wave of light (about 0.4 thousandths of a millimetre) nothing can be seen, so every colour from there on is made up. title: What If You Sank and Couldn't Stop?
description:
You jump off a boat over a coral reef for a swim, and start to sink. You can't swim up. A blue whale rises past you, hammerheads circle you, and the sunlight runs out. You meet a giant squid, an anglerfish, a beaked whale holding its breath, and the Titanic. Then the seafloor ends at a cliff, and you fall into the deepest trench on Earth, onto its floor, and on into the rock beneath it.

What is real: every depth on screen and the animals that live there. Red light is gone from the sea within the first few dozen metres, and almost all sunlight by 200 m. Recreational divers stop at 40 m; the deepest scuba dive ever was 332 m. Below 1,000 m no sunlight has ever reached, and about three in four animals make their own light. A Cuvier's beaked whale has been tracked to 2,992 m. The Titanic lies at about 3,800 m. The deepest fish ever filmed was a snailfish at 8,336 m. The bottom of the Challenger Deep is about 10,935 m down, and a plastic bag has been filmed there. The weight on your fingernail is the real water pressure on one square centimetre: about 385 kg at the Titanic and over a tonne at the bottom.

What is not real, or not known: nobody could survive this, and these places do not line up in one straight drop (the Titanic is in the Atlantic, the Mariana Trench in the Pacific); the cliff beside the Titanic is invented. Real numbers along the way: Formula 1 cars top out around 231 mph. The fastest production car ever, a Bugatti Chiron Super Sport 300+, hit 304 mph in 2019. The fastest train ever tested, Japan's L0 maglev, reached 375 mph in 2015. The land speed record is 763 mph (Thrust SSC, 1997). The SR-71 Blackbird flew 2,193 mph and the X-15 rocket plane 4,520 mph. Driving along the ground at speed v, your weight drops by (v / 17,500 mph)^2: at 17,500 mph you are in orbit. Escape velocity is about 25,000 mph. The Parker Solar Probe, the fastest thing humans have built, reached about 430,000 mph. Light travels at 670,616,629 mph. At 90% of light speed, time in your car runs 2.3 times slower than on Earth; at 99.99%, 70 times slower; at 99.9999999%, about 22,000 times slower (15 days on Earth per minute in the car). No object with mass can reach light speed, and light always passes you at the same speed, however fast you go.

At first it’s just a faint point of light. Then it grows. The stars around it start to bend, its glowing disk stretches across the whole sky, and soon a black hole tens of billions of times heavier than the Sun is hanging over the city.

🕳️ TON 618 facts

Its light has been travelling for about 10.8 billion years to reach us.
It’s estimated at tens of billions of solar masses. The figure you’ll see most often is 66 billion; newer estimates are closer to 40 billion.
Its event horizon is wide enough to swallow our whole solar system many times over.
The glowing disk around it is a quasar, one of the brightest objects in the universe.

This is a visualization. The real TON 618 is billions of light-years away and isn’t coming toward us.

title: What If You Could See Everyone's Search History?
description:
What if you could see everyone's search history? This what if animation gives you five days: every morning, the search bar above everyone's head shows a little more. First their last search, then the whole day, the whole week, the deleted ones, and finally incognito.

Imagine you wake up on Monday, and there's a search bar above everyone's head. Max, two meters of muscle: how to make friends when everyone is scared of you. Chloe, the most popular girl in school: how to look like I don't care. And Ava? Ava searched you.

Along the way, the real side of search: why so many searches are brand new, how "anonymous" searches exposed a real person in 2006, what incognito actually hides, and how long deleted history really takes to disappear.

title: What If You Could See Who Loves You?
description:
What if you could see who loves you? This what if animation gives you three days of hearts above everyone's head: who hates you, who doesn't care, and who loves you 100%.

Imagine you wake up tomorrow, and there's a heart above everyone's head. Black means they don't like you. Gray means you don't matter to them. Red means they like you. And 100% means they're in love with you.

But there's a catch: day one, you only see black hearts. Day two, gray. Day three, red. Then they vanish for a whole year. Your best friend turns out to be at −100%. And the person who loves you 100% is the last person you'd ever guess.

Along the way, the real science of how to tell if someone likes you: a real smile versus a polite one, pupils that widen, and why believing someone likes you can make it come true.

So... whose heart would you check first? Tell us in the comments.

title: What If You Could Smell Everything... and Couldn't Turn It Off?

title: What If You Could Hold Your Breath for an Hour?

Your body does three things that are real somewhere on Earth: the giant spleen of the Bajau sea nomads, the dive reflex that slows your heart in cold water, and the oxygen-packed muscles of Weddell seals. But there's one rule. Your hour only works if you're calm. Get scared, and it becomes ten minutes.

At first it's brilliant. Forty years of wishes from the bottom of the fountain, the swim-class record nobody will ever beat, a ninety-foot quarry and a dog under the ice of Miller's Pond. Then comes the hospital in Denver, where the doctor thinks the machine is broken. And the cost: you sink like a stone, your hands are always freezing, and your ears never stop hurting.

Six years later, one February morning, a minivan punches through the ice of the river. There's a boy in the back seat. And under the ice, it's pitch black...
